A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LLM-GS research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching across relocations and renumbering.

before.justification: v2 reports original Karel benchmark results, language and search ablations, experiments on two newly designed tasks, and LLM program-revision experiments.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds Minigrid experiments, scheduler-component ablations, elapsed-time evaluation, and statistical analyses.

M1.justification: The original Pythonic-DSL initialization and Scheduled HC procedure are retained. Appendix L adds an implemented Minigrid DSL with parameterized object-type/color perceptions, an object-carrying check, and actions including toggle. This is a limited extension of the policy language and its generation/search interface.

E1.justification: v2 evaluates Karel, Karel-Hard, and two novel Karel tasks. v3 retains this coverage and adds Minigrid LavaGap, PutNear, and RedBlueDoor, introducing lava avoidance, object relocation, and ordered opening of colored doors in another environment.

E2.justification: The main Karel comparison retains LEAPS, HPRL, CEBS, and HC. Appendix E/Figure 14 additionally compares the original scheduler against seven alternative component combinations. This expands the ablation comparators; the Minigrid evaluation reuses HC rather than introducing another external baseline.

E3.justification: The original Karel protocol remains unchanged. The new Minigrid protocol uses GPT-4o, 16 environment variants, and a 10,000-program budget, with documented task and reward modifications (Appendix L). Appendix I also introduces elapsed-time evaluation including LLM generation time, extending evaluation beyond program counts.

E4.justification: v3 retains the existing ablations and adds a 2×2×2 study of interpolation, scheduling, and progress-ratio choices on DoorKey and CleanHouse (Appendix E, Figure 14). It also tests whether sample-efficiency advantages translate into elapsed-time advantages on DoorKey, including LLM generation overhead (Appendix I, Figure 18).

E5.justification: Both versions report repeated-seed results and uncertainty displays. v3 adds Student's t-tests, p-value curves, and a 0.05 threshold across all ten original benchmark tasks (Appendix J, Figure 19). Existing Karel run counts are unchanged. The stated null hypothesis is inconsistent with the interpretation assigned to small p-values.

E6.justification: v3 adds Minigrid learning curves, scheduler-variant results, runtime results, and significance outcomes. It reports no significant differences among eight scheduler variants and final superiority over HC on eight of ten tasks in Appendix J. Section 5.2 changes DoorKey convergence from approximately 50K to 500K evaluations; the corresponding Figure 4 curves and Table 3 values are unchanged.

T1.justification: The original scheduler equations remain unchanged. Appendix E.2 adds mathematical definitions of linear alternatives for neighborhood interpolation, scheduling, and progress ratio, particularly Equations 5, 7, and 9. These are limited formal additions supporting the ablations; no theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and concluding contribution summary retain the same central claims: task-aware LLM initialization, Pythonic-DSL generation, Scheduled HC, improved sample efficiency, and natural-language task specification. The additional experiments broaden the evidence supporting this framework without redefining those central contributions.

C2.justification: Appendix E.1 adds substantive reasoning connecting scheduler choices to task difficulty, AST structure, and stable neighborhood sizes early and late in search. Section 3 also qualifies the initialization-distance argument from a direct upper bound to a possible one. The limitations concerning domain experts, suitable DSLs, and capable LLMs are retained.

D1.justification: Appendix L supplies substantial new reproducibility information: Minigrid conversion rules and sampling probabilities, task configurations and rewards, model settings, full prompts, and an example response. Appendix B additionally identifies the off-the-shelf Karel parser. Existing Karel prompts, conversion examples, and post-processing rules are retained.

R1.justification: v3 adds Minigrid-related references, Student (1908), and Zhong et al. (2023), and removes Section 2's explicit 'first attempt' novelty wording. Earlier neural program-synthesis references are largely relocated to Appendix A rather than removed. The broader research positioning remains stable.

P1.justification: Most existing prose is retained. v3 moves latent-space, CEM, and CEBS explanations from Section 3 into Appendix F, shortens the method-section heading, clarifies several descriptions, and adds sections for the new studies. It also updates the publication header and correspondence information; this is not an extensive rewrite.

P2.justification: v3 adds scheduler-comparison, runtime, and ten-task statistical plots, plus Minigrid illustrations, performance plots, and DSL tables. Figures 9 and 22 partly redisplay the same Minigrid results. Existing figures are retained with relocations, revised captions, and surrounding layout changes, including moving Figure 3 earlier.

improvement.justification: v3 strengthens validation through Minigrid experiments, scheduler sensitivity analysis, and timing evidence that includes LLM generation. Correcting DoorKey convergence from 50K to 500K also improves agreement with the retained curve. These provide a useful net improvement in coverage and accuracy, but the timing study lacks hardware details and Appendix J's inconsistent null hypothesis limits the reliability of the added statistical argument.
